result: The Kalinago population of Dominica exhibits approximately 55% Native American, 32% African, and 12% European genetic ancestry, representing the highest Native American genetic ancestry among Caribbean populations documented to date. This exceeds previously reported values for Puerto Rico (13%), Tainos (10-15%), Cubans (8%), and other Caribbean populations.
evaluation: Claims C1, C48 are directly supported by ADMIXTURE analysis at K=4-6 (Figure 1), with consistent results from two-stage admixture and local genetic ancestry analyses. Claims C2, C50-C54 are supported by systematic comparison to published Caribbean population data shown in Figure 2. The individual with highest Native American ancestry (94%, C49) provides additional validation. Sample size (n=458) and multiple analytical approaches strengthen these findings.

result: Three albino individuals in the Kalinago population are homozygous for a novel multi-nucleotide polymorphism OCA2NW273KV (allele frequency 0.03, effect size -8 melanin units) located within an ~11 Mb haplotype of African origin. This represents the first reported case of albinism caused by homozygosity for this variant.
evaluation: The causative variant is well-established through multiple lines of evidence: whole exome sequencing (C81-C82), genotype-phenotype correlation showing only NW273KV homozygotes are albino (C84-C86, Table 1), identity-by-descent analysis (C90, Figure 3), and local genetic ancestry confirming African origin (C91-C92, Figure 3). The allele frequency calculation and Hardy-Weinberg prediction (C96) match observed albinism frequency (3/3000). The R305W variant is definitively excluded as causative (C85-C86).

result: Skin pigmentation in the Kalinago population ranges from 20.7 to 79.7 melanin index units (average 45.9 excluding albinos), with the three albino individuals exhibiting the lowest values (20.7-23.8) along with characteristic clinical features including nystagmus, photophobia, blonde hair, and gray irides.
evaluation: Melanin index measurements are supported by standardized skin reflectometry methodology (Materials and methods). The range and distribution are well-documented (Figure 4-supplement 1), and albino phenotypes are comprehensively characterized with both quantitative (MI) and qualitative (clinical, phenotypic) observations. Comparisons to reference populations (East Asian MI=25, European MI=21, C69-C70) provide context.

result: The European-derived hypopigmentation alleles SLC24A5A111T (frequency 0.14, effect size -6 melanin units) and SLC45A2L374F (frequency 0.06, effect size -4 melanin units) show statistically significant associations with skin pigmentation in the Kalinago, with effect sizes consistent with prior studies in admixed populations.
evaluation: Allele frequencies and effect sizes are supported by genotyping data (n=458) and linear regression analysis (Table 2). Only SLC24A5A111T reaches genome-wide significance (C111), which is appropriate given the sample size and allele frequencies. Effect sizes are consistent with published values from African-American (-5 units, C113) and Cape Verde (-5.5 units, C114) populations. The dose-response relationship (homozygotes lighter than heterozygotes, C99) is demonstrated in Figure 4.

result: Native American genetic ancestry independently reduces skin pigmentation by 24-29 melanin units in individuals lacking major European and African hypopigmentation alleles, as demonstrated by regression analysis showing a clear trend toward lighter pigmentation with increasing Native American ancestry.
evaluation: This finding is supported by focused analysis of 279 individuals lacking SLC24A5A111T, SLC45A2L374F, and OCA2NW273KV alleles (Figure 5), showing slope of -24.3 melanin units per unit Native American ancestry (r²=0.27). PC1, strongly correlated with Native American vs African ancestry, shows the lowest p-value in association analysis (C112). The range of 24-29 units (C11, C109) is bounded by slopes versus NAM and AFR ancestry. However, substantial unexplained variance (r²=0.27) and deviations at extreme ancestry values suggest additional complexity.

result: Previously published polymorphisms predicted to affect skin color in Native Americans (including variants near OPRM1, in EGFR, and MFSD12 Y182H) show no detectable association with hypopigmentation in the Kalinago population, indicating that the genetic variants responsible for Native American hypopigmentation remain unidentified.
evaluation: This negative result is supported by association analysis of previously reported variants (Appendix 2-table 1) showing no significant effects, with the lowest adjusted p-value ~0.001, far above significance thresholds. Claims C22-C27 establish the prior literature context. The failure to identify causative variants despite clear ancestry-associated pigmentation effects (C11, C108) is a robust finding, though the authors appropriately note power limitations (C127) and potential for ungenotyped variants (C128).

result: ADMIXTURE analysis at K=3-6 successfully resolves major global population clusters and demonstrates that the Kalinago population represents admixture primarily between Native American, African, and European ancestral populations, with minor contributions (<1%) from Oceanian and Central/South Asian sources.
evaluation: The ADMIXTURE results are clearly presented in Figure 1 and Figure 1-supplement 1, showing expected clustering patterns at different K values. The separation of Native Americans (red) from East Asians (green) at K=4 (C44) is critical for the study's objectives. The appearance of Oceanian (K=5) and Central/South Asian (K=6) clusters is consistent with prior work (C45-C46, citing Li et al. 2008), and their minimal contribution (C47) is appropriately documented.

result: Self-identified 'Kalinago' individuals have significantly higher Native American ancestry (67% vs 51%), lower African ancestry (23% vs 34%), lower European ancestry (10% vs 14%), and lighter skin pigmentation (MI 42.5±5.6 vs 45.8±9.6) compared to 'Mixed' individuals, demonstrating correlation between folk ancestry categories and genetic ancestry.
evaluation: The correlation between self-identification and genetic ancestry is supported by ADMIXTURE analysis of subgroups (Figure 2-supplement 2) and melanin index measurements (Figure 4-supplement 2). The differences are substantial and consistent across multiple ancestry components. However, the authors appropriately note 'considerable overlap' between groups, and the inference of causality (folk categories 'reflected in' genetic differences, C67) should be interpreted cautiously given potential confounding factors.

result: The higher frequency of SLC24A5A111T (0.14) compared to SLC45A2L374F (0.06) in the Kalinago cannot be explained solely by European admixture, as both alleles are nearly fixed in Europeans. Instead, this pattern is consistent with African source populations carrying SLC24A5A111T at moderate frequencies (0.08-0.15 in Mende, Hausa, Mandinka) and low European ancestry (6.5%) in the SLC45A2 chromosomal region.
evaluation: The inference is well-reasoned, combining observed allele frequencies with literature on European (C102) and African (C103-C104) population frequencies, plus local ancestry analysis (C105). However, this remains an inference rather than direct demonstration, as the specific African source populations for the Kalinago are not definitively established. The logic is sound but alternative explanations (e.g., selection, drift) are not fully excluded.

result: One albino individual heterozygous for SLC24A5A111T showed no lighter pigmentation than other albino individuals homozygous for the ancestral allele, consistent with epistasis of OCA2 hypopigmentation over SLC24A5A111T effects.
evaluation: This observation is supported by direct phenotypic comparison among the three albino individuals with different SLC24A5 genotypes. The epistasis interpretation (C107) is reasonable given the severe hypopigmentation caused by OCA2 albinism likely creates a 'floor effect' masking additional hypopigmentation alleles. However, the small sample size (n=3 albinos, n=1 with heterozygous SLC24A5) limits statistical power, and this remains a qualitative observation.

result: The OCA2NW273KV albinism allele was identified through whole exome sequencing after excluding 28 known African/Native American albinism mutations. The variant is found in 1000 Genomes Project individuals from Barbados and Sierra Leone who share a ~1.5 Mb haplotype with the Kalinago. The R305W variant, which co-occurs with NW273KV on the founder haplotype, is incorrectly predicted as pathogenic by computational tools despite population frequency data inconsistent with causative status.
evaluation: The systematic exclusion of known mutations (C80) and whole exome sequencing approach (C81) are appropriate. The identification of NW273KV carriers in 1KGP (C97) and shared haplotype (C98) support African origin and provide independent validation. The critique of pathogenicity prediction tools (C88) is well-founded given R305W frequency >0.10 in multiple populations (C87) predicting >1% homozygotes, far exceeding albinism prevalence. The inference about the founder haplotype (C89) is reasonable but based on limited data.

result: The sampling program encompassed 458 individuals (15% of the Kalinago Territory population, ages 6-93) including all three known albino individuals. The high Native American ancestry is attributed to geographic segregation within the Territory and marriage traditions requiring women who marry non-Kalinago to leave while allowing non-Kalinago spouses of Kalinago men to enter.
evaluation: The sampling methodology is well-documented (C40-C42), representing a substantial population fraction. The inclusion of all known albinos (C41) is critical for the albinism analysis. The marriage tradition claims (C60-C61) are based on personal communication with the Kalinago Council, which is appropriate for ethnographic information. The inference linking these practices to high Native American ancestry (C62) is reasonable but not directly tested. The age distribution (Figure 1-supplement 3) shows good representation across age groups.

result: The single-allele effect size of OCA2NW273KV (-8 melanin units) represents the first population-based measurement for any albinism allele. Albino individuals were on average 10 melanin units lighter than predicted by the additive model, and the R305W variant shows no detectable effect when controlling for NW273KV status.
evaluation: The novelty claim (C122) appears accurate based on literature review. The effect size is derived from linear regression analysis (Table 2) with appropriate statistical methods. The residual analysis (C123) suggests non-additive effects or additional factors in homozygous albinos. The lack of R305W effect (C124) is supported by conditional analysis (Appendix 2-table 1). However, the small number of albino individuals (n=3) and carriers limits precision of these estimates.

result: An independently collected Kalinago sample showed 67% Native American ancestry based on mtDNA haplotype analysis, higher than the 55% autosomal ancestry found in this study, suggesting paternal bias in European and/or African admixture.
evaluation: The comparison to Crawford et al. 2021 (C55) is appropriately cited, and the inference of paternal bias (C56) is reasonable given that mtDNA is maternally inherited. However, the authors note they cannot directly compare maternal to autosomal ancestry in their own sample due to SNP-chip limitations. The difference could also reflect sampling variation, different analytical methods, or true population structure differences between independently collected samples. This interpretation is plausible but not definitively established.

result: The failure to identify Native American hypopigmentation variants may be explained either by multiple variants of small effect sizes individually below detection limits, or by large-effect variants that were not genotyped and are poorly tagged by the SNP array.
evaluation: These are speculative explanations (both explicitly framed as possibilities, C127-C128) for the negative GWAS results. Both are plausible: polygenic architecture with many small-effect variants is common for complex traits, and SNP array coverage limitations are well-known. However, these remain untested hypotheses. The power analysis (Figure 5-supplement 1) suggests the study had reasonable power to detect moderate-to-large effect variants, but the authors appropriately acknowledge limitations. Additional work (whole-genome sequencing, larger samples) would be needed to distinguish these possibilities.

result: Background claims establish that skin pigmentation is polygenic and environmentally influenced, lighter skin evolved convergently in Europeans and East Asian/Native Americans likely due to vitamin D synthesis requirements at northern latitudes, the SLC24A5A111T allele explains ≥25% of African-European pigmentation differences and is nearly fixed in Europeans, but no equivalent large-effect variant has been found in Native Americans or East Asians despite their shared ancestry and divergence ~15 kya.
evaluation: These are literature review claims (C13-C27) establishing context and motivation for the study. All are appropriately cited to primary literature. The claims accurately represent the state of knowledge in the field and provide clear rationale for studying the Kalinago population. These are not novel findings but rather synthesis of prior work.

result: Historical and demographic context: Caribbean islands were inhabited by populations from northern South America before European contact; large numbers of Africans were introduced as slave labor during the Colonial period; Native American ancestry now contributes <15% in most Caribbean populations; Dominica and St. Vincent were last colonized (late 1700s); the British granted the Kalinago a 15 km² reservation in 1903; the population gained legal rights at Independence (1978) and the territory was redesignated in 2015; approximately 3000 Kalinago currently live in the Territory.
evaluation: These historical and demographic claims (C28-C35) are appropriately cited to historical and genetic literature. They provide essential context for understanding the population's unique genetic structure. The population size estimate (C35) is stated as current knowledge. These are background facts rather than novel findings from this study.

result: Background on oculocutaneous albinism: OCA is a recessive trait characterized by visual abnormalities and hypopigmentation caused by mutations in autosomal pigmentation genes, with incidence ~1:20,000 in European populations but much higher (1:5000) in some sub-Saharan African populations.
evaluation: These are well-established facts about albinism (C36-C39) appropriately cited to medical genetics literature. They provide necessary background for interpreting the albinism findings in the Kalinago population. These are not novel findings but standard medical knowledge.

result: During fieldwork, Kalinago community members characterized themselves and others as 'Black,' 'Kalinago,' or 'Mixed' based on perceived genealogical ancestry.
evaluation: This ethnographic observation (C63) is based on direct fieldwork and is appropriately reported as such. It provides important context for the subsequent genetic ancestry analysis by self-identified groups (C64-C67). This is a straightforward observational claim.

result: Comparative pigmentation data: East Asians (MI=25) and Europeans (MI=21) measured with the same equipment in the authors' laboratory; Senoi of Malaysia (MI 24-78, mean 45.7) with admixture from darker Malaysian Negritos (mean 55); Africans in Cape Verde (mean 53.4) and African-Americans (mean 59).
evaluation: These comparative data (C69-C74) are appropriately cited to prior publications, including the authors' own work. They provide essential reference points for interpreting the Kalinago pigmentation measurements. The use of the same equipment for East Asian and European measurements (C69-C70) strengthens comparability.

result: Literature comparison of SLC24A5A111T and SLC45A2L374F effect sizes: SLC24A5A111T shows effect sizes of -7.7 (Crawford et al. 2017) and -3.6 (Martin et al. 2017b) in continental Africans, and ~-3 in the CANDELA study; SLC45A2L374F shows significant effects in African-Americans (Norton et al. 2007) and CANDELA (Adhikari et al. 2019) but not in African Caribbeans (Norton et al. 2007).
evaluation: These literature comparisons (C115-C120) are appropriately cited and provide context for interpreting the effect sizes measured in the Kalinago. The variation in reported effect sizes across studies highlights the value of the current study's measurements. These are accurate summaries of prior work.

result: Melanin index determined from skin reflectance at the inner upper arm is commonly used as a measure of constitutive skin pigmentation.
evaluation: This methodological claim (C129) is appropriately cited to prior literature on pigmentation measurement methods. It justifies the measurement approach used in the study. This is standard methodology in the field.
